_comment: Eastern Cape Department of Education Grade 11 Geography P1 (Climate and Weather, Geomorphology and Geographical Skills and Techniques), November 2024 provincial common examination.
Questions and marking-guideline answers extracted from the text layer of the official PDFs
(paper1.pdf, paper1_memo.pdf) and read against the rendered pages. Figures, maps,
graphs and photographs are described in [FIGURE: ...] brackets inside 'context'. memo_answer is
from the official marking guideline (English); mark allocations such as (2) are kept, one
accepted point per line. Column A/B items use the Grade 12 '[Y ... / Z ...]' style.
FORMAT: Section A Question 1 The Atmosphere (60) and Question 2 Geomorphology (60); Section B
Question 3 Geographical Skills and Techniques (30) on a 1:50 000 topographical map and a 1:10 000
orthophoto map of the Hartbeespoort Dam area. All three questions are compulsory (150). The map
sheets were not published with the paper (only the question paper is in the zip), so map-read
inputs come from the memo's accepted values. Sub-parts (a)/(b) are kept in one entry.

questions.context: 1.4 Refer to the sketch below illustrating Föhn winds. [FIGURE: air rising up the windward side of a mountain (cloud and rain on that side) and descending the leeward side. questions.context: 1.5 Read the extract on drought and desertification. DESERTIFICATION, DROUGHT AND CLIMATE CHANGE: Dryland areas in Africa are under threat from deforestation, soil erosion, nutrient mining, recurrent drought and climate change, potentially resulting in land degradation, desertification, and aggravated poverty. Sustainable agricultural innovations are key to limiting adverse impacts on the environment and on the livelihoods of rural populations.
questions.text: Differentiate between drought and desertification.
questions.topic: Climate and Weather: Droughts and desertification
questions.memo_answer:
Drought refers to a period of abnormal scarcity of rainfall for a period of more than two years (1)
Desertification is a process where once fertile soil becomes arid

questions.topic: Climate and Weather: Droughts and desertification
questions.memo_answer:
Changing patterns of rainfall (2)
Increased evaporation (2)
Reduced cloud cover (2)
High temperatures/ greater amount of sunshine (2)
Shifting of weather systems (2)
Low relative humidity (2)
[ANY TWO]

questions.text: Quote from the extract the consequences of drought.
questions.topic: Climate and Weather: Droughts and desertification

questions.text: Suggest THREE common management strategies to reduce the spread of drought and desertification.
questions.topic: Climate and Weather: Droughts and desertification
questions.memo_answer:
Water restriction should be imposed in urban areas (2)
Reduce the size of cattle herds to work within the land carrying capacity (2)

Make plans in advance to store food and organise alternative food supplies (2)

[ANY THREE]

questions.context: 2.5 Refer to the photograph below on mass movement. STEADY RAINS CAUSING HAVOC ON THE ROADS. [FIGURE: photograph of large boulders and rubble that have fallen from a rock face onto a road, with a road chevron sign in the foreground.] The Department of Transport has urged drivers to be cautious when approaching mountain passes, after rock falls have partially obstructed roads in two parts of the province. A rock fall has partially obstructed the R67 from Makhanda to Fort Beaufort, 40 km from Makhanda according to Department of Transport spokesperson, Unathi Binqose. Binqose urged road users to be extra cautious when approaching mountain passes as there are threats of mudslides. Steady rains in most parts of the province were causing havoc on the roads and mudslides had been reported on the R102 old Cape Town Road near Mondplaas in Humansdorp area as well as the R67 between Makhanda and Fort Beaufort. [Source: talk/the town.co.za//2023/05/14]
questions.text: What is mass movement?
questions.memo_answer:
Mass movement is the movement of loose material down the slope due to the influence of gravity (2)
[CONCEPT]

questions.text: Identify the type of mass movement depicted on the photograph above.
Besides rainfall mentioned in the above extract, explain other possible causes of mass movement.
questions.memo_answer:
Deforestation/ removal of vegetation result in fewer roots to bind the soil (2)
Road construction/ quarrying/ blasting at the foot of the slopes can upset the balance of slopes (2)
Building of holiday resorts or houses on steep slopes causes rocks to be unstable (2)
Removal of minerals in mining activities and dumping of waste material cause unstable mine dumps or land fill sites (2)
Recreational activities like mountain bike, cycling, scenic walk and skiing make roads unstable (2)
Incorrect farming methods result in mass movement (2)
Gradient – rapid movement of material is more on a steeper lope than gentle slope (2)
[ANY TWO]

questions.text: In a paragraph of approximately EIGHT lines, suggest strategies to minimise or prevent effects of mass movement.
questions.memo_answer:
Drilling bolts into the sides of the hill slope (2)
Build gabions or small stonewalls of rocks at the base of a slope (2)
Use of wire mesh to hold rocks in place (2)
Spraying concrete on the sides of slopes to stabilise rock slope (2)
Reduce deforestation (2)
Close roads to ensure the safety of people when the slope becomes unstable (2)
Drainage and run off channelling structures to remove excess water (2)
Plant natural vegetation on slopes (2)
Complete environmental impact assessment (EIA) before any development to see if construction will have any impact on stability of the slope (2)
Cutting and filling slopes to stabilise them (2)
Restriction of activities along the slope (2)
Use early warning systems to detect land movement or instability of the slope (2)
[ANY FOUR]

questions.context: SECTION B. QUESTION 3: GEOGRAPHICAL SKILLS AND TECHNIQUES. GENERAL INFORMATION ON HARTBEESPOORT DAM: Co-ordinates: 25º43'32" S 27º50'54" E. Hartbeespoort Dam (also known as Harties) is an arch type of dam situated in the North West Province of South Africa. It lies in a valley to the south of the Magaliesberg mountain range and north of the Witwatersberg Mountain Range, about 35 kilometres northwest of Johannesburg and 20 kilometres west of Pretoria. In 1923, the Hartbeespoort Dam was completed. It became a popular holiday and weekend destination for the inhabitants of Johannesburg and Pretoria. [Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ Hartbeespoort Dam] The following English terms and their Afrikaans translations are shown on the topographic and orthophoto map: Agricultural holdings - Landbouhoewes; Archaeological site - Argeologiese terrein; Diggings - Uitgrawings; Estate - Landgoed; Golf course - Gholfbaan; Sewerage works - Rioolwerke. | 3.1 MAPWORK SKILLS AND CALCULATIONS
